scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The dance emerged in the early 1990s, with popularity peaking in Los Angeles and the Southwestern United States.
Its exact origin is debated, with sources citing the U.S.-Mexico border area, Jalisco, or Sinaloa.
Early pioneers included dancers such as Popeye, who is credited with creating many of the original steps.
on_screen: Map: Mexico · North America
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The dance is a social and performance style used at concerts, parties, and in organized dance competitions.
It serves as a marker of Mexican-American youth culture from the 1990s.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage: L.A. Banda: Dance of the New L.A. (https://archive.org/details/clloy_000027)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Partners dance in a close hold, with the male dancer holding the female dancer's waist.
The footwork involves small, alternating jumps or gallops that create a side-to-side swaying motion.
The male dancer performs the 'tombé' by dipping the female partner backward with a straight back, then pulling her up.
Watch for Tombé, Caballito.
on_screen: Hero video full screen, 30–45 s (uIF8MrZ2ptA)
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Partnered, moving in place or around the dance floor.
scenes.music: diegetic (the video's own sound), underscore under narration

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The dance is performed to Regional Mexican music, specifically technobanda, charanga, or cumbia banda.
Instrumentation includes electric guitars, synthesizers, and brass instruments, reflecting a fusion of traditional Sinaloan wind music and modern electronic sounds.
Listen for the Electric guitars, Synthesizers, Brass instruments.
The pulse is 2/4.
A driving, fast-paced fusion of traditional Sinaloan brass and modern electronic synthesizers, characterized by a rhythmic, double-time cumbia beat.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Dancers such as Popeye, Escandalo, Veronica, Pollo, Silvia, GalloBanda, Alex El Tio, and Ana Rosa.
Musical groups include Mi Banda El Mexicano, Banda Machos, and Vaqueros Musical.
Related styles include the 'brinquito' and 'caballito', which emphasize trotting steps and small jumps, and the 'quebradita de espinazo'.
The dance evolved from Sinaloan music and cumbia, incorporating elements from rock acrobático, swing, and lindy hop.
on_screen: Names on screen as they are spoken
Variant names as a small list

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Quebradita is variant of Brinquito: Shares similar galloping footwork but lacks the acrobatic tombé.
Quebradita is variant of Caballito: A related style focusing on small, horse-like jumps.
